Write what a web page needs to identify photos with a key's species

Source: R/onnx.R
exportBrowserModel.Rd

Photo identification as suggestSpecies() and identifyPhotos() do it has two halves: the names of the key's results are embedded as texts, and the photo is embedded as an image and compared with them. The text half can be done ahead of time, here; a web page then needs only the image encoder to identify a photo on the visitor's own device, with no server and no upload. This function writes the files such a page loads.

Usage

exportBrowserModel(
  key,
  model,
  dir,
  encoder = NULL,
  prompt = "a photo of %s.",
  textEmb = NULL
)

Arguments

key

A key whose results are the labels.

model

The onnxModel() (or visionModel()) to embed the labels with. It must be the model the image encoder belongs to.

dir

Folder to write to; created if needed.

encoder

The image encoder for the page: NULL copies the image encoder of model (which must then be an onnxModel()); "hub" points the page at that file on the Hugging Face Hub instead of copying it (for a model that came from there); a file path copies that file; a web address (https://...) is written to the manifest as it is.

prompt

The text each name is put into, with %s where the name goes, as in suggestSpecies().

textEmb

Optional text embeddings made earlier, a matrix whose row names are the prompts (from embedTexts() or loadEmbeddings()); the labels are then not embedded again.

Value

The path of model.json, invisibly.

Files written to dir

model.json, the manifest (UTF-8 JSON):

  • format: "dimoose-browser-model"; version: 1.

  • key: desc (the key's description) and taxa (the number of labels).

  • model: arch, pretrained, dim (embedding dimensions), library.

  • image_encoder: file (a file name in dir, or null), url (a web address, or null; one of the two is set), bytes, precision ("int8", "fp16", "fp32" or null if unknown), input (the input's name, "pixel_values"), input_type ("float32"), input_shape ([1, 3, S, S]), output (the output to read, "image_embeds"), normalized (false: divide the output by its length).

  • preprocess, how to turn a photo into the input: resize ("shortest": scale so the shorter side is resize_to pixels, keeping the shape), interpolation ("bicubic"), crop ("center": cut the middle image_size x image_size square), rescale (multiply the 0-255 values by this, 1/255), mean and std (per channel: subtract, then divide), layout ("NCHW"), channels ("RGB").

  • text_embeddings: file ("text_embeddings.bin"), dtype ("float32"), byte_order ("little"), shape ([labels, dim]), order ("row-major": label by label), normalized (true), prompt (the template).

  • labels: one object per row of the text embeddings, in order: taxon (the result as the key's leads write it, which is what to look up in the key), name (the name put into the prompt: the scientific name when the result has one) and prompt (the text that was embedded).

  • logit_scale: 100.

text_embeddings.bin: labels x dim 32-bit little-endian floats and nothing else, row by row; in JavaScript, new Float32Array(await (await fetch(url)).arrayBuffer()).

image_encoder.onnx: the image encoder, unless the manifest gives a url instead.

What the page does

Prepare the photo as preprocess says, run the image encoder (for example with onnxruntime-web), divide image_embeds by its length to get v, and take the dot product of v with each row of the text embeddings. The probability of each label is the softmax of logit_scale times those dot products, which is what suggestSpecies() computes.

Size

The image encoder is the download that matters. Use an "int8" encoder for the web: 96 MB for CLIP ViT-B/32 and 90 MB for BioCLIP as exportOnnxModel() writes them, against about 350 MB unquantised, with the same answers on dimoose's example photos (BioCLIP 2, a larger model, is 310 MB even so). Where that is still too much, "mobileclip-s0" at "fp16" is 23 MB, but it is a general model that does not know species names as BioCLIP does. The text embeddings are tiny (2 KB per label), and are best made with the "fp32" text encoder: onnxModel(name, precision = "int8", textPrecision = "fp32").

Tested with onnxruntime-web

The "int8", "fp16" and "fp32" encoders that exportOnnxModel() writes for CLIP ViT-B/32 and BioCLIP were run in onnxruntime-web 1.31.1 on its WebAssembly backend (under Node.js) from folders this function wrote, with the 14 Montana example photos prepared as preprocess says. All three load and run there. Against the same file run in Python the lowest cosine of the embeddings was 0.9996 for "int8" and 1.0000 for "fp16" and "fp32", and the most likely label was the same for every photo. The "int8" files hold 8-bit weights that are turned back into floats when the model loads, so they use no integer arithmetic a runtime might lack. The WebGPU backend was not tested.

Ready-made _quantized files from the Hub (encoder = "hub" with an "int8" model) are quantised differently, with integer arithmetic. That of Xenova/clip-vit-base-patch32 had a lowest cosine of 0.85 with the "fp32" embeddings on the same backend and gave another most likely label for 5 of the 14 photos; its "fp16" file had 1.0000. Point a page at the "fp16" file, or copy in an "int8" encoder from exportOnnxModel().

How the photo is resized matters more than the encoder's precision. preprocess$interpolation names the filter the model was trained with (bicubic, with smoothing when a photo is made smaller, as the Python library Pillow does it). With BioCLIP on the Montana photos, resizing with a bilinear filter instead gave embeddings with a cosine of 0.93 to 0.98 (0.97 on average) with the right ones, and nearest-neighbour 0.84 to 0.95.

See also

onnxModel(), exportOnnxModel(), suggestSpecies().

Examples

if (FALSE) { # \dontrun{
model <- onnxModel("bioclip", precision = "int8", textPrecision = "fp32")
exportBrowserModel(montanaKey(), model, "site/model")
list.files("site/model")   # image_encoder.onnx, model.json, text_embeddings.bin
} # }
